st.ask.body: Ask about the basics of Ramadan, fasting, prayer or being a new Muslim. For rulings and personal situations, ask your local imam.
st.ask.label: Your question
st.ask.ph: e.g. What do I say when I break my fast?
st.g.what.t: What Ramadan is and why we fast
st.g.what.p1: Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. It is the month in which the Quran was first sent down (Quran 2:185). All month, Muslims fast each day from dawn until sunset: no food, no drink and no marital relations in those hours.
st.g.what.p2: Fasting in Ramadan is one of the five pillars of Islam (Bukhari 8). Allah tells us the reason: fasting was prescribed 'that you may become righteous' (Quran 2:183). The Arabic word is taqwa, which means being mindful of Allah in what you do and what you leave.
st.g.what.p3: So Ramadan is more than an empty stomach. It is a month to pray, read the Quran, give and guard your tongue. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever fasts Ramadan with faith, hoping for Allah's reward, will have their past sins forgiven (Bukhari 1901).
st.g.who.t: Who has to fast, and who is excused
st.g.who.p1: Fasting Ramadan is a duty for every adult Muslim who is sane and well enough to fast. If you are a new Muslim, you fast from now on. You do not owe the Ramadans from before your Islam, because Islam wipes out what came before it (Muslim 121).
st.g.who.p2: Allah gives ease to people in difficulty. Someone who is ill or travelling may leave the fast and make up the same number of days later (Quran 2:184). A woman does not fast during her period or bleeding after childbirth, and makes those days up afterwards (Muslim 335). A woman who is pregnant or nursing may leave the fast if she fears harm for herself or her baby (Tirmidhi 715). Scholars differ on what she does afterwards, so ask your local imam.
st.g.who.p3: A very old person, or someone with a lasting illness who can never fast, feeds a poor person for each day instead (Quran 2:184, Bukhari 4505). This is called fidya. Your mosque can tell you the amount.
st.g.who.p4: Children do not have to fast until they reach puberty (Abu Dawud 4403). Many practise with a few days, as the children of the Companions did (Bukhari 1960). If you are unsure whether you are excused, ask an imam and your doctor.
st.g.day.t: What a fasting day looks like
st.g.day.p1: The day begins before dawn with suhoor, a meal eaten before the Fajr prayer time. The Prophet ﷺ said, 'Take suhoor, for there is blessing in it' (Bukhari 1923). Even a little food and water counts.
st.g.day.p2: You need to intend the fast before dawn (Abu Dawud 2454). It is in your heart, with no words needed. Getting up for suhoor because you mean to fast is already an intention.
st.g.day.p3: From the start of Fajr until sunset (Maghrib) you do not eat or drink (Quran 2:187). School, work and prayers carry on as normal. Use the prayer times from your local mosque or this app.
st.g.day.p4: When the sun sets, break your fast straight away (Bukhari 1957). This is iftar. The Prophet ﷺ used to break his fast with dates, or with water if there were none (Abu Dawud 2356). When he broke his fast he said: 'Dhahabaz-zama'u wabtallatil-'uruqu wa thabatal-ajru in sha' Allah', which means 'The thirst is gone, the veins are moistened, and the reward is confirmed, if Allah wills' (Abu Dawud 2357). Then pray Maghrib and eat your meal.
st.g.breaks.t: What breaks the fast and what does not
st.g.breaks.p1: Three things break the fast when done on purpose between dawn and sunset: eating, drinking and marital relations (Quran 2:187). Making yourself vomit on purpose also breaks it (Tirmidhi 720). If a woman's period begins during the day, that day's fast ends and she makes it up later (Muslim 335).
st.g.breaks.p2: Eating or drinking because you truly forgot does not break the fast. The Prophet ﷺ said such a person should complete the fast, 'for what he has eaten or drunk has been given to him by Allah' (Bukhari 1933). Stop when you remember and carry on. Being sick without meaning to does not break it either (Tirmidhi 720).
st.g.breaks.p3: Having a shower or bath is fine (Bukhari 1926). So is rinsing your mouth, as long as you do not swallow the water (Abu Dawud 2385). In wudu, just do not sniff water deep into your nose while fasting (Tirmidhi 788). Swallowing your own saliva is fine. You can clean your teeth if you swallow nothing. Many people keep toothpaste for before dawn and after sunset to be safe.
st.g.breaks.p4: Scholars differ about inhalers, injections, drops and other medical matters. Ask your local imam, and never stop a medicine without asking your doctor.
st.g.breaks.p5: A fast can also lose its reward. The Prophet ﷺ warned that Allah has no need of a person leaving food and drink if they do not leave lying and bad behaviour (Bukhari 1903).
st.g.missed.t: If you miss a day or break your fast
st.g.missed.p1: If you missed days for a good reason, such as illness, travel or your period, you make up one day for each day missed (Quran 2:184). Making up a fast is called qada. Try to finish them before the next Ramadan, as Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, did (Bukhari 1950).
st.g.missed.p2: If you broke a fast on purpose without a good reason, do not give up. Turn back to Allah, ask His forgiveness and make the day up. Breaking the fast by marital relations during the day carries a heavy penalty as well (Bukhari 1936). Scholars differ on some of these details, so speak to your local imam about what you owe.
st.g.missed.p3: One bad day does not spoil your Ramadan. Fast the next day, and write down any days you owe so they are not forgotten.
st.g.prayers.p1: The five daily prayers are a duty all year, and they matter more than any extra worship in Ramadan. Allah says in a hadith that nothing brings His servant closer to Him than the duties He has set (Bukhari 6502). If you are new to prayer, make the five prayers your first goal.
st.g.prayers.p2: Tarawih is an extra night prayer in Ramadan, prayed after Isha. It is a sunnah, not a duty. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever stands in prayer in Ramadan with faith, hoping for reward, will have their past sins forgiven (Bukhari 37).
st.g.prayers.p3: Tarawih is prayed two rakahs at a time. The number of rakahs differs between mosques, so simply follow your imam. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever stands with the imam until he finishes has the reward of praying the whole night (Tirmidhi 806). You may also pray it at home. If you get tired, pray what you can.
st.g.quran.t: Reading the Quran when you are new
st.g.quran.p1: Ramadan is the month of the Quran (Quran 2:185). The angel Jibril met the Prophet ﷺ every night of Ramadan to go through the Quran with him (Bukhari 6).
st.g.quran.p2: If you cannot read Arabic yet, read a translation in your own language. Listening to a reciter while you follow the meaning helps too. Learn the Arabic letters with a teacher when you can.
st.g.quran.p3: Do not worry about finishing the whole Quran in your first Ramadan. Choose a small amount you can keep up every day, even one page or ten minutes. The Prophet ﷺ said that the person who reads the Quran with difficulty has a double reward (Bukhari 4937).
st.g.last-ten.t: The last ten nights and Laylatul Qadr
st.g.last-ten.p1: The last ten nights are the best part of Ramadan. When they began, the Prophet ﷺ worked harder in worship, stayed up at night and woke his family (Bukhari 2024).
st.g.last-ten.p2: One of these nights is Laylatul Qadr, the Night of Decree. Allah says it is 'better than a thousand months' (Quran 97:3). We are not told which night it is. The Prophet ﷺ said to look for it in the odd nights of the last ten (Bukhari 2017). Whoever stands in prayer on that night with faith, hoping for reward, has their past sins forgiven (Bukhari 1901).
st.g.last-ten.p3: Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, asked what to say on that night. The Prophet ﷺ taught her: 'Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun tuhibbul-'afwa fa'fu 'anni', which means 'O Allah, You are Pardoning and You love to pardon, so pardon me' (Ibn Majah 3850).
st.g.last-ten.p4: You do not need to stay awake all night. Pray Isha and Fajr on time, pray some extra rakahs, read some Quran, and make dua in your own words on each of the ten nights.
st.g.charity.p1: The Prophet ﷺ was the most generous of people, and he was most generous of all in Ramadan (Bukhari 6). Giving does not have to be money. Sharing food counts: whoever gives a fasting person food to break their fast earns the same reward as that person (Tirmidhi 807).
st.g.charity.p2: At the end of Ramadan there is a special charity called zakat al-fitr. It is a set amount, measured in food, given to the poor for every member of the family, young and old, and it must be given before the Eid prayer (Bukhari 1503). Most mosques collect it and announce the amount for each person, so ask yours how and when to pay.
st.g.charity.p3: Ramadan lasts 29 or 30 days, and the day after it ends is Eid al-Fitr. Nobody fasts on Eid (Bukhari 1990). The Prophet ﷺ ate some dates before going out to the Eid prayer (Bukhari 953). Wear your best clean clothes, pray the Eid prayer with the community, thank Allah for guiding you (Quran 2:185) and enjoy the day.
st.g.family.t: When your family or colleagues are not Muslim
st.g.family.p1: Many new Muslims fast in a home, school or office where nobody else does. It can feel lonely, but you can do it. Tell people simply and calmly: 'I am fasting for Ramadan, so I will not eat or drink until sunset.' Most people respect a clear, friendly answer.
st.g.family.p2: Plan ahead. Put something easy for suhoor by your bed or in the fridge the night before. Carry dates and water in case you are out at iftar. At work or school, ask politely for a quiet place to pray.
st.g.family.p3: Keep good relations with your parents and family, even if they do not agree with your faith. Allah tells us to keep company with our parents 'with appropriate kindness' (Quran 31:15). When Asma asked whether she should be good to her mother, who was not a Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ said, 'Yes, keep good relations with her' (Bukhari 2620). Eat with them in the evening when you can, help at home, and let your good manners speak for you. If someone argues with you, the Prophet ﷺ taught us to say, 'I am fasting' (Bukhari 1904).
st.g.family.p4: Find company too. Look for a mosque or a community iftar near you, and ask one Muslim friend to be your Ramadan buddy who checks in with you each day.
st.g.mosque.t: Your first visit to a mosque and a community iftar
st.g.mosque.p1: Anyone may walk into a mosque. Dress modestly in clean clothes. Take off your shoes at the door and put them on the rack. There is a washing area for wudu. Most mosques have separate prayer areas for men and women.
st.g.mosque.p2: Inside there are no reserved seats. Sit on the carpet wherever there is room. If you are able, pray two rakahs before you sit down (Bukhari 444). When the prayer starts, stand shoulder to shoulder in the row and follow the imam. Put your phone on silent.
st.g.mosque.p3: At a community iftar, people usually break the fast with dates and water at the call to prayer, pray Maghrib together and then eat the meal. You do not need an invitation or money. Feeding a fasting person is something people are glad to do (Tirmidhi 807).
st.g.mosque.p4: It is fine to ask. Tell someone, 'I am new, can you show me what to do?' People are usually delighted to help a new Muslim.
st.g.gentle.p1: You do not have to do everything in your first Ramadan. Start with what is required: the fast and the five prayers. Then add one or two small things, such as a page of Quran each day.
st.g.gentle.p2: Small and steady is better than big and short. The Prophet ﷺ said that the deeds Allah loves most are the regular ones, even if they are small (Bukhari 6464). He also said that the religion is easy, and that whoever makes it too hard on himself will not be able to keep going (Bukhari 39).
st.g.gentle.p3: You will make mistakes. Everyone does. When you slip, ask Allah to forgive you and carry on the same day. Allah says He 'does not charge a soul except with that within its capacity' (Quran 2:286), and that He intends ease for you and not hardship (Quran 2:185).
st.pr.i1: Salah is the prayer a Muslim offers five times a day. It is the second pillar of Islam (Bukhari 8) and it has set times (Quran 4:103). It is a few minutes of standing, bowing and prostrating before Allah. The Prophet ﷺ said, 'Pray as you have seen me praying' (Bukhari 631).
st.pr.i2: A prayer is made of units called rakahs. Fajr, before sunrise, has 2 rakahs. Dhuhr, just after midday, has 4. Asr, in the afternoon, has 4. Maghrib, just after sunset, has 3. Isha, at night, has 4.
st.pr.i3: Before you pray, be clean. Make wudu, and make sure your body, your clothes and the place where you pray are clean. Dress modestly, and stand facing the Qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Makkah (Quran 2:144). A compass app or your local mosque can show you the direction. A woman does not pray during her period and does not make those prayers up (Muslim 335).
st.pr.i4: The steps below show the prayer in a simple form. The four schools of law agree on the main actions, and differ in a few small details of position and wording. Follow the way your teacher or local mosque shows you.
st.w.w1.x: Intend in your heart that you are making wudu for prayer. Say 'Bismillah' (in the name of Allah) and use clean water.
st.w.w2.x: Wash both hands up to the wrists three times, getting water between your fingers.
st.w.w3.x: Take water into your mouth, swirl it and spit it out, three times. When fasting, take care not to swallow any.
st.w.w4.x: Sniff a little water gently into your nose and blow it out, three times. When fasting, do not sniff deeply.
st.w.w5.x: Wash your whole face three times, from the hairline to the chin and from ear to ear.
st.w.w6.x: Wash your right arm from the fingertips up to and including the elbow three times. Then do the same with your left arm.
st.w.w7.x: Wet your hands and wipe them over your head. Then wipe the inside and back of your ears with your wet fingers.
st.w.w8.x: Wash your right foot up to and including the ankle three times, with water between the toes. Then do the same with your left foot.
st.w.w9.x: The Quran names washing the face, washing the arms, wiping the head and washing the feet. The other steps follow the way the Prophet ﷺ made wudu. Washing once is enough, and three times is the sunnah. Your wudu lasts until you use the toilet, pass wind or fall into a deep sleep. Schools differ on a few other things, so ask your local imam.
st.p.p1.x: Stand facing the Qibla. Know in your heart which prayer you are about to pray, for example Fajr. You do not need to say the intention aloud.
st.p.p2.x: Raise both hands and say the takbir. The prayer has now begun, so do not talk or look around. Most Muslims then place the right hand over the left, and some leave their arms at their sides. Do as your teacher shows you.
st.p.p3.x: Standing, recite Surah Al-Fatiha, the first chapter of the Quran. It has seven ayat and is part of every rakah. After it, say 'Ameen'. In the first two rakahs, then recite another short surah or a few ayat that you know. Schools differ on what you recite when praying behind an imam, so ask your teacher.
st.p.p3.m: In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. The Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful. Master of the Day of Judgement. It is You we worship and You we ask for help. Guide us to the straight path. The path of those You have favoured, not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who have gone astray.
st.p.p4.x: Say 'Allahu Akbar' and bow, with your hands on your knees and your back level. Stay until your body is still, and say these words. Three times is common.
st.p.p4.m: Glory be to my Lord, the Almighty.
st.p.p5.x: Rise from bowing, saying the first phrase as you come up. Stand fully straight and still, and say the second phrase.
st.p.p5.m: Allah hears the one who praises Him. Our Lord, to You belongs all praise.
st.p.p6.x: Say 'Allahu Akbar' and go down so that your forehead and nose, both palms, both knees and the toes of both feet rest on the ground. Stay until you are still, and say these words. Three times is common.
st.p.p6.m: Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.
st.p.p7.x: Say 'Allahu Akbar' and sit up. Rest until you are still, with your hands on your thighs. You can ask Allah for forgiveness here.
st.p.p8.x: Say 'Allahu Akbar' and prostrate a second time, saying the same words as in the first sujood. That completes one rakah.
st.p.p8.m: Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.
st.p.p9.x: Say 'Allahu Akbar' and stand up. The second rakah is the same as the first: Al-Fatiha, another short passage, ruku, standing, and two sujood with a sitting between them. The only difference is that you do not raise your hands for an opening takbir again.
st.p.p10.x: After the second sujood of the second rakah, stay sitting and say the tashahhud. This wording is the one taught in Bukhari 831. Some schools teach another wording that is also from the Prophet ﷺ, so learn the one your teacher uses. In Maghrib, Dhuhr, Asr and Isha, then say 'Allahu Akbar' and stand for the third rakah. In the third and fourth rakahs, recite Al-Fatiha only.
st.p.p10.m: All greetings, prayers and good things are for Allah. Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings. Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah. I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger.
st.p.p11.x: In the last rakah of any prayer, sit after the second sujood and say the tashahhud again. Then ask Allah to send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ with these words, and make a short dua if you wish. If you have not learned these words yet, say what you know and keep learning with your teacher.
st.p.p11.m: O Allah, send Your mercy upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You sent Your mercy upon Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim. You are the Praiseworthy, the Glorious. O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim. You are the Praiseworthy, the Glorious.
st.p.p12.x: Turn your head to the right and say the salam, then turn to the left and say it again. The prayer is complete.
st.p.p12.m: Peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah.
st.pr.note: This is a simple outline and cannot replace a teacher. Ask your local mosque or a Muslim you trust to pray beside you and correct you gently. The positions of the hands and feet and some of the words differ slightly between the schools of law, so follow the way you are taught. Praying imperfectly while you learn is still prayer. Do not wait until you know everything before you begin.
st.term.suhoor.d: The meal eaten before dawn, before a day of fasting begins.
st.term.iftar.d: Breaking the fast at sunset, and the meal eaten then.
st.term.salah.d: The prayer a Muslim offers five times a day, with set actions and words.
st.term.fajr.d: The dawn prayer, 2 rakahs, prayed between first light and sunrise. The fast starts when its time begins.
st.term.dhuhr.d: The midday prayer, 4 rakahs, prayed after the sun passes its highest point.
st.term.maghrib.d: The sunset prayer, 3 rakahs. The fast ends when its time begins.
st.term.isha.d: The night prayer, 4 rakahs, prayed once the sky is fully dark.
st.term.wudu.d: Washing the face, arms, head and feet in a set way before prayer.
st.term.rakah.d: One unit of prayer: standing, bowing once and prostrating twice.
st.term.qibla.d: The direction Muslims face in prayer, towards the Kaaba in Makkah.
st.term.ruku.d: Bowing in prayer, with the hands on the knees.
st.term.sujood.d: Prostration: placing the forehead, nose, hands, knees and toes on the ground in prayer.
st.term.sunnah.d: Extra prayers the Prophet ﷺ prayed regularly before or after the five daily prayers. They bring reward and are not obligatory.
st.term.witr.d: A night prayer with an odd number of rakahs, prayed after Isha and before Fajr.
st.term.tarawih.d: The extra night prayer of Ramadan, prayed after Isha, usually together in the mosque.
st.term.tahajjud.d: A voluntary prayer in the night, usually after sleeping and before Fajr.
st.term.duha.d: A voluntary prayer in the morning, after the sun has risen and before midday.
st.term.dua.d: Asking Allah for something, in any language and at any time.
st.term.dhikr.d: Remembering Allah, often by repeating short phrases of praise such as Subhanallah and Alhamdulillah.
st.term.adhkar.d: The plural of dhikr. It often means the set words of remembrance for the morning, the evening and after prayer.
st.term.istighfar.d: Asking Allah for forgiveness, for example by saying Astaghfirullah.
st.term.salawat.d: Asking Allah to send blessings and peace upon the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.
st.term.tadabbur.d: Thinking carefully about the meaning of the Quran as you read or listen.
st.term.khatm.d: Completing a reading of the whole Quran from beginning to end.
st.term.juz.d: One of the thirty equal parts of the Quran. Reading one a day completes the Quran in a month.
st.term.taqwa.d: Being mindful of Allah, so that you do what pleases Him and keep away from what does not.
st.term.ikhlas.d: Sincerity: doing a good deed only for Allah.
st.term.riya.d: Showing off: doing a good deed so that people will see it and praise you.
st.term.muhasaba.d: Looking back honestly over your day to see what went well and what to put right.
st.term.gheebah.d: Backbiting: saying something about a person behind their back that they would dislike, even if it is true.
st.term.sadaqah.d: Voluntary charity. It can be money, food, help or even a kind word.
st.term.zakat-al-fitr.d: A set charity of food given for each member of the family at the end of Ramadan, before the Eid prayer.
st.term.qada.d: Making up a missed fast or prayer on a later day.
st.term.fidya.d: Feeding a poor person for each day missed, for someone who can never fast because of old age or lasting illness.
st.term.hayd.d: A woman's monthly period. She does not pray or fast during it, and makes up the fasts afterwards.
st.term.laylatul-qadr.d: The Night of Decree, when the Quran was first sent down. It is better than a thousand months and falls in the last ten nights.
st.term.itikaf.d: Staying in the mosque for a time to worship Allah, especially in the last ten days of Ramadan.
st.term.hilal.d: The thin new crescent moon. Seeing it marks the start of Ramadan and the start of Eid.
st.term.eid-al-fitr.d: The day of celebration after Ramadan, the first day of the month of Shawwal. It begins with the Eid prayer.
ks.1.x: Allah made the first human, Adam, and taught him the names of all things. The angels did not know these names. They said they only knew what Allah had taught them. Then Adam told them the names. Allah told the angels to bow down before Adam. They all did, except Iblis. He was proud and refused. Adam and his wife lived in the Garden. They could eat from wherever they liked, but Allah told them not to go near one tree. Shaytan made them slip. Then Allah taught Adam words to say, and Allah accepted his repentance. When we do something wrong, we can turn back to Allah too. He is the Most Merciful.
ks.1.q: What happened after Adam turned back to Allah?
ks.2.x: Prophet Muhammad told his companions about a man who was walking and became very thirsty. He found a well, climbed down into it and drank. When he came out, he saw a dog. It was panting and licking the wet earth because it was so thirsty. The man thought that the dog felt just as he had felt. So he climbed down the well again, filled his shoe with water, held it in his mouth, climbed up and gave the dog a drink. Allah thanked him for this and forgave him. The companions asked if there is a reward for being kind to animals. The Prophet said that there is a reward for kindness to every living creature.
ks.2.q: What did the man use to carry water to the dog?
ks.3.x: Prophet Nuh called his people to worship Allah alone, but only a few believed. Allah told Nuh to build a ship. Whenever the leaders of his people walked past, they laughed at him. Nuh kept building. Then the command of Allah came, and the water rose. Allah told Nuh to bring a pair of every kind of creature onto the ship, along with his family and the believers. Nuh told them to go on board in the name of Allah. The ship sailed through waves like mountains. Then the water went down, and the ship came to rest on a mountain called Judi. Allah kept Nuh and the believers safe. Nuh did what Allah asked, even when people made fun of him.
ks.3.q: What did Allah tell Nuh to build?
ks.4.x: Some good deeds look very small. Prophet Muhammad taught his companion Abu Dharr not to think of any good deed as too small, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face. The Prophet did this himself. A companion called Jarir said that from the day he became a Muslim, every time the Prophet saw him, he greeted him with a smile. The Prophet also said that a good word is charity. So you do not need money to give something. A kind word and a happy face are gifts. Today you can give them to your family, your friends and your neighbours, and Allah sees every one of them.
ks.4.q: What small good deed did the Prophet tell Abu Dharr not to look down on?
ks.4.a: Meeting others with a cheerful face.
ks.5.x: The people of Prophet Ibrahim prayed to statues that they had made. Ibrahim knew that only Allah should be worshipped. One day, when the people had gone away, he broke the statues into pieces, all except the biggest one. When the people came back, they were angry and asked Ibrahim if he had done it. He told them to ask the statues, if they could speak. The people knew very well that statues cannot speak. Ibrahim asked them why they worshipped things that could not help them or harm them. They were furious and decided to burn him. But Allah said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim." Allah kept him safe.
ks.5.q: What did Allah tell the fire to be?
ks.6.t: Hajar and the Water of Zamzam
ks.6.x: Prophet Ibrahim brought Hajar and their baby Ismail to a dry valley in Makkah. Nobody lived there and there was no water. Hajar asked him, "Has Allah ordered you to do so?" He said, "Yes." She said, "Then He will not neglect us." Soon their water was finished, and the baby was very thirsty. Hajar climbed the hill of Safa to look for help. She saw nobody. She ran to the hill of Marwa. She went between the two hills seven times. Then she saw an angel at the place of Zamzam, and water came out of the ground. She drank and fed her baby. Today, pilgrims walk between Safa and Marwa, just as Hajar did.
ks.6.q: How many times did Hajar go between Safa and Marwa?
ks.7.x: When Ismail grew up, he and his father, Prophet Ibrahim, did a great work together. They raised the walls of the Kaaba in Makkah, the House of Allah. As they built, they made dua. They said, "Our Lord, accept this from us. Indeed, You are the Hearing, the Knowing." They also asked Allah to make them and their children people who obey Him, and to accept their repentance. Think about that. They were doing one of the best deeds ever, yet they did not boast. They asked Allah to accept it. When you fast, pray or help someone this Ramadan, you can ask the same: O Allah, please accept this from me.
ks.7.a: Prophet Ibrahim and his son Ismail.
ks.8.x: A king named Heraclius once heard about Prophet Muhammad and wanted to know more. Some traders from Makkah were in his land. Their leader, Abu Sufyan, was not a Muslim at that time. He was against the Prophet. The king asked him many questions. One was whether the people had ever known Muhammad to tell lies before he said he was a prophet. Abu Sufyan answered, "No." The king asked if he broke his promises. Again the answer was, "No." The king asked what he taught. Abu Sufyan said that he told people to worship Allah alone, to pray, to speak the truth and to be good to their relatives. Even those who were against the Prophet knew that he was truthful.
ks.8.q: What did Abu Sufyan say when asked if the Prophet had ever told lies?
ks.9.x: When Yusuf was a boy, he had a dream. He saw eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowing down to him. His father, Prophet Yaqub, told him not to tell his brothers. But the brothers were already jealous, because they felt their father loved Yusuf more. They asked to take Yusuf out to play. Then they put him at the bottom of a well. They brought their father his shirt with false blood on it and said a wolf had eaten him. Yaqub did not believe them. He chose to be patient and asked Allah for help. Some travellers found Yusuf in the well and took him to Egypt. Allah was looking after Yusuf the whole time.
ks.9.q: What did Yusuf see in his dream?
ks.9.a: Eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowing down to him.
ks.10.x: Many years passed. Yusuf grew up in Egypt, and Allah gave him a high position. He was put in charge of the storehouses of the land. One day his brothers came to Egypt, asking for food. They did not know who he was. At last Yusuf told them, "I am Yusuf." The brothers were ashamed and said that they had done wrong. Yusuf could have punished them. But he said, "No blame will there be upon you today. May Allah forgive you." Then his parents came to Egypt, and the family was together again. Yusuf said that his dream had come true and that Allah had been good to him. Forgiving others is a great deed.
ks.10.q: What did Yusuf do when his brothers said they had done wrong?
ks.11.t: Your Mother, Your Mother, Your Mother
ks.11.x: A man came to Prophet Muhammad with a question. He wanted to know which person most deserved his good company and kind treatment. The Prophet said, "Your mother." The man asked, "Who is next?" The Prophet said, "Your mother." The man asked again, "Who is next?" The Prophet said, "Your mother." The man asked a fourth time, and the Prophet said, "Your father." Our mothers carried us, fed us and cared for us when we could do nothing for ourselves. Our fathers work hard for us too. In Ramadan, you can help set the table for iftar, tidy up without being asked, and speak gently to your parents. These are deeds that Allah loves.
ks.11.q: How many times did the Prophet say "Your mother" before he said "Your father"?
ks.12.x: When Musa was a baby, his people were in danger from Pharaoh, a cruel king. Allah inspired Musa's mother to feed her baby and, when she feared for him, to put him into the river. Allah told her not to fear or be sad, and promised to bring him back to her. The family of Pharaoh found the baby. Pharaoh's wife asked that he be kept safe. Musa's sister followed and watched from far away. The baby would not feed from any nurse. So his sister offered to show them a family who could care for him. In this way, Allah returned Musa to his own mother. The promise of Allah is always true.
ks.12.q: Who watched baby Musa from far away?
ks.13.x: Allah told Prophet Musa to leave Egypt by night with his people. Pharaoh and his army chased after them. In the morning, the two groups could see each other. In front of Musa's people was the sea. Behind them was the army. The people cried out that they were sure to be caught. Musa said, "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me." Then Allah told Musa to strike the sea with his staff. The sea split apart, and each side stood like a huge mountain. Allah saved Musa and everyone with him. Pharaoh and his army were drowned. When things look impossible, remember Musa's words and trust Allah.
ks.13.q: What did Musa strike the sea with?
ks.14.x: Abu Talha was a companion in Madinah who owned many date palm gardens. The one he loved most was called Bayruha. It was in front of the Prophet's mosque. Prophet Muhammad used to go there and drink its sweet water. Then Allah sent down an ayah saying that we will never reach true goodness until we give from what we love. Abu Talha came to the Prophet. He said that Bayruha was the thing he loved most, and that he wanted to give it away for the sake of Allah. The Prophet was pleased and told him to share it among his relatives. So Abu Talha did. Real giving means sharing something we love, not only what we no longer want.
ks.14.q: What was the name of the garden Abu Talha gave away?
ks.15.x: Prophet Yunus was sent to his people, but he left them in anger. He got on a ship that was full. Lots were drawn, and Yunus was the one who had to leave the ship. Then a great fish swallowed him. Inside the darkness, Yunus called out to Allah: "There is no god except You. Glory be to You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers." Allah heard him and saved him. The fish put him out onto the shore. He was weak, and Allah made a plant grow over him. Then Allah sent him to a people of a hundred thousand or more, and they believed. Allah says that this is how He saves the believers.
ks.15.q: Where was Yunus when he called out to Allah?
ks.15.a: Inside the great fish, in the darkness.
ks.16.x: A hungry man came to Prophet Muhammad. The Prophet had nothing at home but water, so he asked who would host this guest. A man from the Ansar, the Muslims of Madinah, said that he would. At home, his wife told him they had only enough food for their children. They put the children to sleep. They set the food in front of the guest. Then the wife stood up as if to fix the lamp, and put it out. In the dark, the two of them pretended to eat, so that the guest could eat it all. They went to sleep hungry. In the morning, the Prophet told the man that Allah was pleased with what they had done.
ks.16.q: Why did the family put out the lamp?
ks.16.a: So the guest would not see that they were not eating, and could have all the food.
ks.17.x: Ayyub was a prophet of Allah. A great hardship came to him. He did not turn away from Allah. He turned to Him. He called out, "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful." Allah answered his dua. Allah told him to strike the ground with his foot. A spring of cool water came out, for him to wash with and to drink. Allah took away his hardship and gave him back his family, and as many again with them, as a mercy. Allah says about Ayyub, "Indeed, We found him patient, an excellent servant." When something is hard for you, be patient like Ayyub and keep asking Allah.
ks.18.x: Aishah once asked Prophet Muhammad if he had ever had a day harder than the battle of Uhud. He told her about a day when he had invited some people to Islam and they refused to listen. He walked away full of sadness. Then he looked up and saw a cloud shading him, and in it was the angel Jibril. Jibril told him that Allah had heard what the people said, and had sent the Angel of the Mountains. The angel offered to bring two mountains down upon those people if the Prophet wished. The Prophet said no. He said that he hoped Allah would bring from their children people who would worship Allah alone. He chose mercy.
ks.18.q: What did the Prophet hope for the children of those people?
ks.18.a: That they would worship Allah alone.
ks.19.x: Allah gave Prophet Sulayman a great kingdom. His army had jinn, people and birds, all marching in rows. Allah had also taught him the speech of birds. One day the army came to a valley of ants. One ant called out, "O ants, enter your homes, so that Sulayman and his soldiers do not crush you without knowing it." Sulayman understood her, and he smiled. He did not feel proud of his power. He made dua at once. He asked Allah to help him be thankful for the blessings given to him and to his parents, and to help him do good deeds that please Allah. The more Allah gives us, the more we should thank Him.
ks.19.q: What did Sulayman do when he heard the ant?
ks.19.a: He smiled and asked Allah to help him be thankful.
ks.20.t: The Young People of the Cave
ks.20.x: Long ago, some young people believed in Allah, but their people worshipped other things. The young people stood up and said that their Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. To keep their faith safe, they went to a cave. They made dua: "Our Lord, grant us from Yourself mercy and prepare for us right guidance in our affair." Allah made them sleep in the cave. Their dog lay at the entrance with its front legs stretched out. When they woke up, they thought they had slept for a day or part of a day. But Allah tells us they had been there for three hundred and nine years. Allah protects those who hold on to their faith.
ks.20.q: How long did the young people stay in the cave?
ks.21.x: Allah gave a man named Luqman wisdom. The Quran tells us the advice he gave his son. First, he told him never to worship anything along with Allah. He told him that even if a deed is as small as a mustard seed, hidden inside a rock or anywhere in the heavens or the earth, Allah will bring it out. He told him to pray, to encourage what is right, to stop what is wrong, and to be patient. He told him not to turn his face away from people with pride, and not to walk in a boastful way. He told him to walk calmly and to lower his voice. Which piece of this advice can you practise today?
ks.21.q: How small a deed did Luqman say Allah will bring out?
ks.21.a: Even one as small as a mustard seed.
ks.22.t: Maryam and the Gift from Allah
ks.22.x: Before Maryam was born, her mother made a promise. She promised that her child would be given to the service of Allah. When the baby came, she named her Maryam and asked Allah to protect her. Allah accepted Maryam and made her grow up in a good way. Prophet Zakariyya looked after her. Maryam worshipped Allah in her prayer room. Every time Zakariyya came in to see her, he found food with her. He asked, "O Maryam, where does this come from?" She said, "It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without limit." Maryam knew that every good thing we have comes from Allah. Do you remember to thank Him for your food?
ks.22.q: Where did Maryam say her food came from?
ks.23.x: Allah gave Maryam a son, Isa, as a sign and a mercy. When she carried the baby to her people, they were very surprised and began to question her. Maryam did not answer. She only pointed to the baby. They asked how they could speak to a child in the cradle. Then, by the power of Allah, baby Isa spoke. He said, "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet." He said that Allah had made him blessed wherever he was, had told him to pray and give charity, and had made him good to his mother. Isa was a noble prophet and a servant of Allah.
ks.23.q: What was the first thing baby Isa said about himself?
ks.23.a: That he is the servant of Allah.
ks.24.t: Ten Years Without a Harsh Word
ks.24.x: When Prophet Muhammad came to Madinah, a boy named Anas was brought to him. His family said that Anas was a clever boy who could help the Prophet. So Anas served him, at home and on journeys. Later, Anas told people what those years were like. He said, "I served the Prophet for ten years, and he never said to me, 'Uff.'" The Prophet never blamed him by asking, "Why did you do that?" or "Why did you not do that?" Think about how gentle that is. Children make mistakes, and the Prophet was always patient with Anas. We can copy him by being patient with our younger brothers, sisters and friends.
ks.24.q: For how many years did Anas serve the Prophet?
ks.25.x: Before he became a prophet, Muhammad used to go to the cave of Hira to worship Allah alone. One day the angel came to him there and told him to read. He answered, "I do not know how to read." The angel held him tightly and let go, three times. Then the angel recited the first words of the Quran to be revealed: "Read in the name of your Lord who created." The Prophet went home with his heart beating fast. He asked his wife Khadijah to cover him. She comforted him. She said that Allah would never let him down, because he was good to his relatives, helped the poor and was generous to his guests.
ks.25.q: In which cave did the first revelation come?
ks.26.x: The companion Ibn Abbas told us something beautiful about Ramadan. He said that Prophet Muhammad was the most generous of all people. And he was at his most generous in Ramadan, when the angel Jibril met him. Jibril used to come to him every night of Ramadan, and they would go over the Quran together. Ibn Abbas said that the Prophet was then more generous than the wind that blows freely and brings good to everyone. So Ramadan is the month of two things together: the Quran and giving. Tonight, you can read some Quran, even a few ayahs. Then you can give something, even if it is small, like a date, a coin or your help.
ks.26.q: Who met the Prophet every night of Ramadan?
ks.27.x: One night in Ramadan is greater than all the others. It is Laylatul Qadr, the Night of Decree. Allah sent down the Quran on this night. Allah tells us that it is better than a thousand months. That is more than eighty-three years! On this night the angels come down, and Jibril with them, by the permission of their Lord. It is a night of peace until dawn. We are not told exactly which night it is. Prophet Muhammad told us to look for it in the odd nights of the last ten nights of Ramadan. So on these nights, pray, read Quran and make lots of dua. A small deed on this night is worth so much.
ks.27.q: Laylatul Qadr is better than how many months?
ks.28.x: Aishah, the wife of Prophet Muhammad, saw how he prayed at night. He stood in prayer for so long that his feet became sore and cracked. She asked him why he did this, when Allah had already forgiven him. He answered, "Should I not love to be a thankful servant?" The Prophet did not pray only to ask for things. He prayed to say thank you to Allah. Allah has given us so much: our eyes, our families, our food, our faith and this blessed month. We can say thank you with our words by saying Alhamdulillah. We can also say thank you with our actions, by praying and by using our blessings to do good.
ks.28.q: Why did the Prophet pray so much at night?
ks.28.a: Because he loved to be a thankful servant of Allah.
ks.29.x: Prophet Muhammad told his companions about a man who was walking along a road. On the path he saw a branch with thorns. It could have hurt the people passing by. The man did not just step over it and carry on. He picked it up and moved it out of the way. That was all he did. But Allah was pleased with his deed and forgave him. This story shows us that no good deed is too small. Picking up litter, moving a stone off the path or putting away a toy that someone might trip on are all good deeds. You may forget them by the evening, but Allah does not forget.
ks.29.q: What did the man move off the road?
ks.30.x: Ramadan is over, and Eid al-Fitr is here! In the Quran, Allah says that He wants ease for us, not hardship. He wants us to complete the days of fasting, to say how great He is for guiding us, and to be thankful. That is why we say "Allahu Akbar" on Eid. Prophet Muhammad did not go out to the Eid prayer until he had eaten some dates, and he ate an odd number of them. He also came home from the prayer by a different road from the one he took to get there. Today, thank Allah for helping you fast, pray and give. Wear your best clothes, smile and share your joy with others. Eid Mubarak!
ks.30.q: What did the Prophet eat before going to the Eid prayer?
ks.30.a: Some dates, an odd number of them.
